> is this something that it is planned to be implemented in next version of semtools?

It can be in semTools as soon as it is available in lavaan.  As of now, the sampling (co)variances of factor scores are unavailable for factors whose indicators are latent response variables (underlying observed ordinal response variables).  I don't think this is high on Yves' priority list, so it might be available sooner from blavaan, where it is a high priority for the next version (although that could still take quite some time).

> And do plausible values require different assumptions when working with categorical indicators - instead of continuous ones?

The latent response variables are assumed normal, but the fact that they are unobserved adds a layer of complexity to deriving / approximating their sampling variability.

messages.subject_clean: measurement invariance with a single-factor scale and categorical items
messages.body_plain:
> it is ok to remove the intercepts if there is one threshold per item? ...

> I also then tested threshold & loadings invariance, and threshold, loading, & intercept invariance.

With only 1 threshold per item, there is no way to distinguish differences in thresholds, intercepts, or loadings across groups.  So you have to compare your configural model directly to a model with scalar (threshold, loading, & intercept) invariance.  Strict invariance can then still be tested, if you are interested in that.

> Does removing the intercept part prevent comparison among the nested models (i.e., the configural model, threshold invariance model, threshold & loading invariance model, and  threshold, loading, & intercept invariance model)?

No, it just prevents independent identification of different sets of variables.  Thus, you have to simultaneously (not separately) test the assumption of equal thresholds, loadings, & intercepts.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Moderation simsem
messages.subject_clean: Moderation simsem
messages.body_plain:
> I have two endogenous latent variables

Your syntax is correct, except for one detail.  How you set the residual-covariance parameters is to calculate the covariance among their explained variances (i.e., expected values given the common-factor effects):

> endoMat <- matrix(cov(factors$endog1, factors$endog2), ### ??
>                   nrow = 2, ncol = 2,
>                   dimnames = list(c("endog1", "endog2"), c("endog1", "endog2")))
> diag(endoMat) <- c(var(factors$endog1),var(factors$endog2)) ### ??

Even if these were the correct values, it would be sufficient to simply take the covariance matrix returned by cov()

cov(factors[ , c("endog1","endog2")])

But the residual covariance is the unexplained variances.  You can just choose any values you want.  If the explained variances are < 1 and you want the population slopes to be interpretable as standardized slopes, then you can use an identity matrix to calculate 1 minus the explain variance:

exoMat <- cov(factors[ , c("endog1","endog2")])
## subtract from 2 × 2 identity matrix
endoMat <- diag(2) - exoMat
## choose a residual correlation
resCor <- 0.3 # or whatever value you want
## convert to residual covariance by multiplying by the SDs
endoMat[1,2] <- endoMat[2,1] <- resCor * prod(sqrt(diag(endoMat)))

Then this line will correctly simulate the latent-variable residuals:

> uniqueFactors <- data.frame(MASS::mvrnorm(N, mu = rep(0, 2), Sigma = endoMat))

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: Compare non-nested SEM model with binary outcomes
messages.body_plain:
> Or I could just use  fitmeasure() to see  which one has the better fit? (CFI; TLI; RMSEA; SRMR)

Only information criteria (AIC, BIC) and incremental fit indices (CFI, TLI) were developed with the ability to compare non-nested models.  The former are available only with ML estimators, so you could obtain them if you choose estimator = "PML" (pairwise ML).  The latter can only compare models when the same baseline.model= (by default, the independence model) is nested within all competing models.

Bentler, P. M., & Bonett, D. G. (1980). Significance tests and goodness of fit in the analysis of covariance structures. Psychological Bulletin, 88(3), 588–606. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.88.3.588

Katsikatsou, M., Moustaki, I., Yang-Wallentin, F., & Jöreskog, K. G. (2012). Pairwise likelihood estimation for factor analysis models with ordinal data. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis, 56(12), 4243–4258.
PML tutorial: https://users.ugent.be/~yrosseel/lavaan/pml/PL_Tutorial.pdf

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
Dear Terrence,

Thank you very much for your response.

I reconstructed the table adding scaling correction factors and shift parameters. Then, I calculated (standard chi-square/scaling correction factor) + shift parameter in the right edge column. These numbers are about the same as the scaled.chi-square values.

Then, I conducted anova between these two models.

Hello guys,

I hope you are very well.

I know that this forum is only for lavaan and sem related problems, but I turn to you to see if you can help me clarify these doubts. Thanks in advance.

The instrument is a single-item scale designed to measure academic self-efficacy. This item has five options (from 1 = completely disagree to 5 = completely agree) and we want to conduct the analysis using the SEM approach. The problem is that; we have never done an analysis of single-item scale. Our questions are:

01. Is it necessary or pertinent to conduct a CFA in order to validate the factorial structure of such a scale? We guess that this isn’t necessary because the scale has only one item.

02. Is it relevant or correct to perform an invariance analysis in order to establish differences in latent factors? (In this case, there is only one construct which is academic self-efficacy). We wonder if working with scales like this permits the SEM approach or, otherwise, generalized linear models (ANOVA, ANCOVA, t-test) should be used.

03. How can we obtain the estimates of the latent construct (academic self-efficacy) by SEM approach? The traditional way of doing this is by summing or averaging the items, which is then compared to some pre-established scale. How could this be done using SEM?

We would really appreciate your help.

Best regards.

fit <- sem(model, data = PoliticalDemocracy)

Many thanks

messages.subject: Re: Psychometric analysis of single-item scale
messages.subject_clean: Psychometric analysis of single-item scale
messages.body_plain:
Juan,

I don't see how you could do any of those things in a CFA/SEM context with a single item.

The closest you could come as far as I can think of is to do #2 with a cumulative/ordered probit regression, as you suggest--that models the ordered categories as coarse cuts on a latent normal distribution. But that would only test differences in location. It would assume invariance.

polr() in MASS could do this, or clm() in ordinal. sem() in lavaan could, but unless you have missing data that's using a sledge hammer on a gnat. I don't know enough to recommend any of these over the other from a technical standpoint.

Pat

messages.subject: Re: CFA using DWLS based on polychoric correlations or full weight matrix?
messages.subject_clean: CFA using DWLS based on polychoric correlations or full weight matrix?
messages.body_plain:
There are simulation results that suggest that you don't necessarily need to run an ordinal / categorical model with a 7-point scale on your indicators. However, this depends on the symmetry of the distribution.

I believe that Weighted Least Squares estimation always uses polychoric correlations for the sample covariance matrix, by the way. That's how the parameters are estimated. Using the full weight matrix (instead of just the diagonal) for standard errors and adjusting the test statistic is done after parameters are estimated (since one needs estimates to compute a fit function).

- the : for interactions only works with observed variables, not factors
- if you want to create an interaction factor and predict it, my best guess is that the product indicator approach is the best option. You can follow the examples from the indprod() function in semTools
- when you say "I am also interested in how the interaction between these two factor scores depend on another variable W.". It sounds to me that you should do a three way interaction instead, as this addresses how a 2 way interaction is affected by a third variable. Instad of predicting the product term

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I used indProd() function to run moderation analysis using R Lavaan and semTools packages.

The analysis ran smoothly. However I came across following issue:
If I use MLM estimator in the sem() function,  for e.g.,
> fit2 <- sem(moderationmodel, estimator="MLM", data = moderationdata,std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, meanstructure = TRUE)

Then I get following warning message:
Warning message:
In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov)
    does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue
    (= -1.999005e-17) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that
    the model is not identified

When I inspected this using following:
> lavInspect(fit2, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>")
I get following output:
                  IV         MOD    DV     IVXMOD
IV             1.000
MOD        0.567  1.000
DV            0.977  0.932  2.183
IVXMOD -0.521 -0.467 -0.719  1.000

However, if I don't use any estimator (which defauls to ML estimator), then I get no warning message despite the same output of variance-covariance matrix as follows:
> fit2 <- sem(moderationmodel, data = moderationdata,std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, meanstructure = TRUE)
> lavInspect(fit2, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>")
                  IV         MOD    DV     IVXMOD
IV             1.000
MOD        0.567  1.000
DV            0.977  0.932  2.183
IVXMOD -0.521 -0.467 -0.719  1.000

The summary() function runs alike with same results in either case.
So what does this mean? Since I have used MLM in my CFA and SEM path analysis (due to violation of multivariate normality, I preferred it to default ML estimator, and MLM has given much better model fit results); don't I have to use the same estimator in my moderation analysis?

Also here are the slope outputs:
$SimpleSlope
      MOD     Slope            SE                   Wald       p
[1,]  -1        0.7653475   0.07849022 9.750865 0.0e+00
[2,]   0        0.5972600   0.07190843 8.305841 0.0e+00
[3,]   1        0.4291725   0.10532919 4.074583 4.6e-05

And attached is the plot (Rplot):

Although I understand from this (and attached plot) that as the moderator increases the impact of IV upon DV decreases, still I would appreciate some source to understand/interpret SimpleSlope outputs shared above in detail. Also, in marketing journals, the moderation analysis is generally represented as showcased in the two attached examples (Moderation examples 1 and 2) herewith. I have used values of moderator as showcased by default in probe2WayMC() function as valProbe(-1,0,1). Does it mean that this is showcasing moderator at means and -1 standard deviation, + 1 standard deviation levels? Or it simply means low, mean, and high moderator levels?

messages.subject: Re: Ordinal variables in lavaan: Difference between ordered=TRUE and estimator=DWLS
messages.subject_clean: Ordinal variables in lavaan: Difference between ordered=TRUE and estimator=DWLS
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I think your answer may be down the bottom here: https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html

Such that in specifying order = TRUE, you're getting the mean and variance adjusted test statistic and the full weight matrix (rather than diagonalized) is used for the parameter estimates. When specifying DWLS, without the ordered argument, those two things down happen, thus different fit measures (fit function) and different parameter estimates.

As far as what to use, that's your choice! If you want to truly model the indicators as ordinal, I'd go with ordered = TRUE.

-R

messages.subject: Re: Moderation simsem
messages.subject_clean: Moderation simsem
messages.body_plain:
If you want to set standardized population parameters, the total variance must be 1, in which case any subset (explained or unexplained) must be < 1.  If your explained variance > 1, then your slopes are not standardized.  They don't have to be.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics

messages.subject: Re: How to interpret change of scaled.chi-square values between models?
messages.subject_clean: How to interpret change of scaled.chi-square values between models?
messages.body_plain:
> factorial invariance model was significantly worse than the configural invariance model. Is my interpretation right?

Yes.

> We should use standard chi-square values for model comparison instead of using scaled chi-square values.
>
> Is my understanding right?

Yes, on the contingency that you do a robust correction by scaling the difference between standard chi-squared values.

>
>
>
> These values showed that the factorial invariance model was better than the configural invariance model.

The chi-squared test stat shows you the factorial invariance fits worse, to a statistically significant degree, than the configural model.  The RMSEA shows that decrement in fit is less than is expected given the increase in df.  The CFI/TLI show that factorial invariance improves on the independence model relatively more than the configural model (where "relative" is in terms of the change in df).

> Although these findings contradicted the previous ones of the chi-square difference test

It is not a contradiction.  If these fit measures all quantified the same thing, there would not be multiple fit measures.  They are quantifying different aspects of (mis)fit, and they are all vague because they try to boil down everything that is wrong with your model into a single number.  Try instead looking at local indices of misfit, by running lavResiduals(), which gives you an idea how poorly your model(s) reproduce each mean, variance, and correlation in your data.

> we should judge which model is better comprehensively with theoretical consideration. Is my understanding right?

That plays an important role, but the data can provide evidence against your theory.  Your theory should guide your choice of what evidence you look for in the data to challenge your preconceptions (null hypotheses).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Even with normal data (which match Chen's conditions), Chen's (or any) rules of thumb derived do not provide consistent decisions across a variety of data and model characteristics. > The smallest eigenvalue
>     (= -1.999005e-17) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that
>     the model is not identified

It is a warning that there might be a problem, not an error that there was one.  If your estimates and SEs make sense, then it is probably not an issue.  The smallest eigenvalue is essentially zero, indicating some multicollinearity in the sampling variances of your estimated parameters (not the parameters themselves).

> When I inspected this using following:
> > lavInspect(fit2, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>")

That is a function of model parameters, not what the message referred to.

eigen(lavInspect(fit2, "vcov"))
# or merely
eigen(vcov(fit2))

> However, if I use ML estimator, then I get no warning message. So what does this mean?

The linear dependency doesn't exist in the estimated sampling covariances of estimated parameters if you assume normal data; only when using the robust SEs, which are the square-roots of the diagonal of vcov(fit2)

I see, I will post here an example of the code for others who may have encountered the same problem. The code is for illustrative purpose, please feel free to amend it.

# Get data for interaction factor
data.interac <- indProd(PoliticalDemocracy,var1 = c('x1','x2','x3'), var2 = c('y1','y2'), match=FALSE, meanC=FALSE, residualC=FALSE, doubleMC=FALSE)

# define sem model
model <- '
  # latent variable definitions

     ind60 =~ x1 + x2  +x3

     dem60 =~ y3 + y4 +y5
     ind=~y1 + y2
# define interaction factor
ind60ind =~ x1.y1 +x1.y2+x2.y1+x2.y2 +x3.y1 +x3.y2
  # regressions
    dem60 ~ ind60+ ind+ ind60ind
'
# estimate model
sem_model <- sem(model, data=data.interac, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE)

Dear Prof Jorgensen;

I am conducting a research about violence in couples and I am aplying APIM model. I have 2 exogenous variables, 2 mediators and 3 dependent variables (5 endogenous). Each variables has several subscales?. It is necessary to split all variables by gender to conduct APIM model.
My strategy is :
- Collapse all items of subscales in a observable variable. I mean each subscale only will have a value (the average of values of people's answer)
- All exogenous variables will be correlated
-Residual error will be correlated.
- Each variable (subscale) has to be related with endogenous variable both for man and women of each couple(following APIM model)
- Assess each exogenou variable in different models, one for each exogenou variables.
I am coming up that both models are saturated and I can't know if the model converges or fit.
I tried it with the 2 exogenous variables at the same time and I have the same problem. The model is saturated.
Apart of this, can I extract conclusion about "effects" between variables" despite to the model is saturated?
Is this plan correct?
Any thought to improve the model?
Would be necessary to simply it, eliminating any variables?
Can I do this kind of model (APIM) with so amount of variables?

Thanks in advance.

David Vilariño
Universidad de Jaén
Spain

messages.body_plain:
> I have used values of moderator as showcased by default in probe2WayMC() function as valProbe(-1,0,1). Does it mean that this is showcasing moderator at means and -1 standard deviation, + 1 standard deviation levels?

Not necessarily.  The values in the help-page example were arbitrary, as they probably must be when dealing with latent variables.  But if you want to probe at the mean +/- 1 SD, then you can obtain them from your model output.  lavInspect(fit2, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>") already showed you that the variances are 1 (so their square-roots are also 1).  You can find the latent-variable means the same way: lavInspect(fit2, "mean.lv <http://mean.lv>")

If those are in fact M=0 and SD=1, then you already have probed the simple slopes at the M +/- 1 SD of the moderator.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Changes in Parameters and R2 once Mediation is introduced?
messages.subject_clean: Changes in Parameters and R2 once Mediation is introduced?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to understand to which extent psychological factors mediate the association between parental and offspring education and stumbled into some strange results I can't really make sense of.

Consider a simplified model

s5_co_highest_edu ~ s2_co_factor_ability + s3_co_factor_scholastic_motivation   + s3_pa_edu

Fitting this in lavaan leads to a rather satisfying R2 of 0.44 which is identical to what I obtain when I estimate it using OLS. The parameters are matched as well between both approaches.

But then I introduce a mediation of the form

s2_co_factor_ability ~  s3_pa_edu
s3_co_factor_scholastic_motivation  ~ s3_pa_edu
s5_co_highest_edu ~ s2_co_factor_ability + s3_co_factor_scholastic_motivation   + s3_pa_edu

While the parameters are still the same, the R2 is reduced by 0.03, down to 0.41.

The whole thing gets even stranger if I want to model  s5_co_highest_edu not as continuous but instead as ordinal. It looks to me like the correlations in your raw data are low, possibly because your indicators are not very reliable (although it's hard to tell without more information about the model and data).

There's not a lot you can do about that, in terms of model fitting, as it means your data are not very suitable for this analysis.

I think you should write about what you have learned, and if you were given time and resources, what you would do differently if you were able to start again.

Jeremy

messages.subject: Re: Plot interaction
messages.subject_clean: Plot interaction
messages.body_plain:
For the betas, you use the estimates from the summary() or parestimates() function from lavaan. for the parameter covariance you can use the vcov(fit) function, this will give you he variance/covariance matrix between parameter. You can subselect only the parameter you need to see the smaller matrix with the parameters you need

How many categories does your outcome has? I think you can still use this, because lavaan will give you the probit regression for categorical outcome. And the probit estimate is still an estimate of the linear relation, but linear with the ojive transformation. So, the visualization will present the linear probist relation, which can be hard to interpret.

Another option would be to estimate the simple slopes for the values of interest. And then use those estimates to transform the probit estimates to probabilities, and create the change in probablity plots on your own for each probit simple slopes. This woul be more coding work, but would lead to more meaningful plots

messages.subject_clean: Model Statistic = 0 and 0 DF?
messages.body_plain:
Nothing is going wrong. This happens when you have a saturaded model, this means that you are estimating as many parameters as unique elements from your data covariance matrix. When you have a saturated model you are replicating all the elements of the coavriance matrix, so you have df=0, and the model cannot estimate fit indices (more like have perfct prediction of the coavriance matrix)

messages.subject: Error Message for Multigroup SEM analysis
messages.subject_clean: Error Message for Multigroup SEM analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone!

A few months ago when I ran my code, I obtained better fit indices and never once experienced the following error code:

lavaan WARNING: using a single label per parameter in a multiple group setting implies imposing equality constraints across all the groups; If this is not intended, either remove the label(s), or use a vector of labels (one for each group); See the Multiple groups section in the man page of model.syntax.lavaan WARNING: some estimated ov variances are negativelavaan WARNING: some estimated lv variances are negative

Now that I am revisiting my analyses - that message popped up and my fit indices tanked (CFI now = .875; CFI back then = .91)

Below is my model code.
My question is, has anyone experienced this? By chance is there a solution to this error message that may be worsening my fit indices?

NeighInflu=~1.0*PhysDis
NegPerCh=~1.0*Impul
NegPerCh=~1.0*Unemo
PeerInf=~1.0*PerDel

NeighInflu=~NeighInflu_Alc*Alc
NegPerCh=~NegPerCh_Alc*Alc
PeerInf=~PeerInf_Alc*Alc

Marij~Alc_Marij*Alc

NeighInflu~~VAR_NeighInflu*NeighInflu
PhysDis~~VAR_PhysDis*PhysDis

NegPerCh~~VAR_NegPerCh*NegPerCh
Impul~~VAR_Impul*Impul
Unemo~~VAR_Unemo*Unemo

PeerInf~~VAR_PeerInf*PeerInf
PerDel~~VAR_PerDel*PerDel

Alc~~Var_Alc*Alc
Marij~~VAR_Marij*Marij

NeighInflu~~NegPerCh
NeighInflu~~PeerInf
NegPerCh~~PeerInf

Marij~~Age
Alc~~Age

PhysDis~1;
Impul~1;
Unemo~1;
Alc~1;
Marij~1;
'
mymodel.6.fit<- cfa(mymodel.6,
                     data=project,
                    group = "Race",
                    fixed.x=FALSE, estimator = "MLR", missing="FIML")

summary(mymodel.6.fit,
        rsquare=TRUE,
        standardized=TRUE,
        fit.measures=TRUE)

fitmeasures(mymodel.6.fit, c("cfi", "rmsea","tli",estimator="MLR"))

Best,
Sarah

messages.subject: Re: Correlation Matrix
messages.subject_clean: Correlation Matrix
messages.body_plain:
The covariance is the estimated statistic, and the p-values are for it (specifically, the test of the covariance against the null that it is zero). The correlation is a number derived from three estimated statistics (the covariance and the two variances), so, if you're able to test the covariance--as in SEM--a p for the correlation would have no real added value. (We learn in first-year stats how to generate a p-value via a t-test of a correlation coefficient, but that's usually from a much simpler "model," and it takes into account the sample size in a more direct way.)

Correlations are just an easily interpretable effect size, as Mauricio said. I don't personally know many people who can draw meaning from glancing at a variance/covariance matrix.

Pat

messages.subject: Bias in latent mean and variance in longitudinal data
messages.subject_clean: Bias in latent mean and variance in longitudinal data
messages.body_plain:
I have simulated (using mirt) a longitudinal dataset consisting of 2 measurements with a 10 item scale, using the same item parameters at each measurement. The latent mean at Time 1 was set at 0 and the variance at 1. The latent mean at Time 2 was set at 0.5, its variance at 2, and the correlation between Time 1 and Time 2 was set at 0.70.
I subjected this dataset to a 2-factor analysis in lavaan, with factors T1 and T2 and the appropriate items loading on these factors. The loadings and thresholds of the same items were constrained to be equal over time. The latent mean and variance of T1 were fixed at 0 and 1. The latent mean and variance of T2 were freely estimated, as was the covariance between T1 and T2. Residual correlations between same items across time were allowed. I used the following command.
fit <- lavaan(model, data=datw, ordered=names(datw))
I got the following:
Warning message:
In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov)
    does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue
    (= 1.988158e-22) is close to zero. This may be a symptom that the
    model is not identified.
However, the parameters and their SEs seem OK (except that there are no SEs reported for the item variances).
The latent mean of T2 is estimated to be 0.20 (instead of the simulated 0.50) and the latent variance of T2 is estimated to be 1.32 (instead of the simulated 2).
My questions are:
- Does the warning message indicate there is something wrong with the data or the model?
- If not, what explains that lavaan does not recover the simulated latent mean and variance of T2?
Thanks, Berend

Seconding Pat, in short, we report the p-value and test the unstandardized parameter, but can use the correlation for easier interpretation.

On Saturday, May 22, 2021 at 1:19:30 PM UTC+2 Pat Malone wrote:
> The covariance is the estimated statistic, and the p-values are for it (specifically, the test of the covariance against the null that it is zero). The correlation is a number derived from three estimated statistics (the covariance and the two variances), so, if you're able to test the covariance--as in SEM--a p for the correlation would have no real added value. (We learn in first-year stats how to generate a p-value via a t-test of a correlation coefficient, but that's usually from a much simpler "model," and it takes into account the sample size in a more direct way.)

> Correlations are just an easily interpretable effect size, as Mauricio said. I don't personally know many people who can draw meaning from glancing at a variance/covariance matrix.

> Pat

Thanks for your thoughts.
You have a point that I had not included across time indicator covariances in the simulation model. These covariances were all small and not (highly) significant:

   .Item_10.1        -0.007    0.007   -0.959    0.337

I repeated the analysis excluding the across time indicator covariances from the model. This did not change the latent mean (0.200) and variance for T2 (1.326).

I don't think chance fluctuation can explain the departure of my results from the simulated population values. Note that I had simulated 20,000 simulees.

The question is still open: Why does lavaan fail to estimate the simulated latent mean (0.5) and variance (2.0) of the Time 2 factor?
Berend

library(mirt)

set.seed(12345)

nitems <- 10          # number of items per scale

b2  <- c(-0.8, -0.8, -0.4, -0.4, 0, 0, 0.4, 0.4, 0.8, 0.8)
bc <- b2/4
b1 <- b2 - 1 + sample(bc)
b3 <- b2 + 1 + sample(bc)
a1 <- sample( 1.7+b2/2 )

cf.simb <- as.matrix( data.frame(a1,b1,b2,b3) )
cf.simb <- as.data.frame(cf.simb)

# Transform b-parameters to d-parameters (mirt works with d-parameters)
# difficulty (b) = easiness (d) / -a

cf.sim <- cf.simb

colnames(cf.sim) <- c("a1","d1","d2","d3")

cf.sim$d1 <- -cf.simb$b1*cf.sim$a1
cf.sim$d2 <- -cf.simb$b2*cf.sim$a1
cf.sim$d3 <- -cf.simb$b3*cf.sim$a1

### Simulate dataset using 'mirt'

a1 <- as.matrix(cf.sim[ , 1])
d1 <- as.matrix(cf.sim[ , -1])

# Create theta T1 and dat1 (baseline)

N <- 20000         # sample size

set.seed( sample(10000:20000,1) )

tet1s <- rnorm(N, 0, 1)          # simulate theta T1
tet1s <- as.matrix(tet1s)

dat1 <- simdata(a1, d1, N, itemtype="graded", Theta=tet1s)
dat1 <- as.data.frame(dat1)

# Create theta change

tetchs <- rnorm(N, 0.5, 1)

# Create theta T2 and dat2  (follow-up)

tet2s <- as.matrix(tet1s + tetchs)     # theta T2
# mean(tet2s)
# var(tet2s)

set.seed( sample(30000:40000,1) )

dat2 <- simdata(a1, d1, N, itemtype="graded", Theta=tet2s)
dat2 <- as.data.frame(dat2)

datw <- data.frame(dat1, dat2)

messages.body_plain:
Valeria,

First, MLR is not robust to all kinds of non-normality (e.g., zero-inflation, outliers). Though it will still probably be better than ML.

Second, yes, you're probably stuck with DWLS regardless. One option to consider, depending on the variable's nature, is binning your outcome (making it ordinal). What is the DV?

Pat

>

> What estimator should I use in this situation?

messages.body_plain:
Berend

First about data simulation. I would recommend to use a multivruate for simulation of thetas. Like this

cov2cor(rbind(c(1, 0.99),
              c(0.99, 2)) )

thetas <- rockchalk::mvrnorm(n=N, mu=c(0, 0.5), Sigma = rbind(c(1, 0.99),
                                                              c(0.99, 2)) )

Next, by simulating them separately
dat1 <- simdata(a1, d1, N, itemtype="graded", Theta=as.matrix(thetas[,1]) )
dat1 <- as.data.frame(dat1)

Dear all,

I am slowly but surely getting forward. Can you please help me with two more things?

First, am I right to believe that the means and intercepts of latent variables are arbitrary (in my case with the variance of the intercept and slope fixed to 1) and not directly interpretable (e.g. the intercept is not the mean of time point one)?

Second, I have been asked to compare my linear growth model to intercept-only and curvilinear models to provide a rationale for this approach.

I started by running the linear growth model, added a quadratic model and an intercept-only model, and compared the fits using lavTestLRT.
Is this the "correct" procedure?

Unfortunately, the quadratic model (2.) results in a warning:

In lav_object_post_check(object) :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated lv variances are negative

And this results in a warning when comparing the fits:
In lavTestLRT(fit_strong_boredom_growth, fit_strong_boredom_growth_q,  :
  lavaan WARNING: some models have the same degrees of freedom

Is there an error in my quadratic model?

Thank you very much and kind regards,
Manuel

messages.body_plain:
Dear Terrence,

Thank you very much for your response.

According to your suggestion, “Try instead looking at local indices of misfit by running lavResidual(),”

I run lavResiduals().

I have four groups, each of which has a standardized residual matrix for covariance (cov.z).

But, it seems to be difficult for me to deal with all of them.

Is lavResiduals() similar to modificationIndices()?

It seems to me that these functions give us only the misfit information in each group.

I think that both lavResiduals() and modificationIndices() cannot show which equal constraint worsen the fit.

Is my understanding right?

I need the information of misfit between groups.

Would you please tell me where I can get such information?

Sincerely yours,

Hideki
2021年5月14日金曜日 12:05:33 UTC+9 Terrence Jorgensen:

> > factorial invariance model was significantly worse than the configural invariance model. Is my interpretation right?
>
> Yes.
>
> > We should use standard chi-square values for model comparison instead of using scaled chi-square values.
> >
> > Is my understanding right?
>
> Yes, on the contingency that you do a robust correction by scaling the difference between standard chi-squared values.
>
> >
> >
> >
> > These values showed that the factorial invariance model was better than the configural invariance model.
>
> The chi-squared test stat shows you the factorial invariance fits worse, to a statistically significant degree, than the configural model.  The RMSEA shows that decrement in fit is less than is expected given the increase in df.  The CFI/TLI show that factorial invariance improves on the independence model relatively more than the configural model (where "relative" is in terms of the change in df).
>
> > Although these findings contradicted the previous ones of the chi-square difference test
>
> It is not a contradiction.  If these fit measures all quantified the same thing, there would not be multiple fit measures.  They are quantifying different aspects of (mis)fit, and they are all vague because they try to boil down everything that is wrong with your model into a single number.  Try instead looking at local indices of misfit, by running lavResiduals(), which gives you an idea how poorly your model(s) reproduce each mean, variance, and correlation in your data.
>
> > we should judge which model is better comprehensively with theoretical consideration. Is my understanding right?
>
> That plays an important role, but the data can provide evidence against your theory.  Your theory should guide your choice of what evidence you look for in the data to challenge your preconceptions (null hypotheses).
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

Dear Terrence

Thank you very much for your answer! I have another brief question concerning the pooling, but this time the pooling of goodness-of-fit indices.

By accident, I found that for example the CFI for each single imputed set is around 0.95 to 0.96 (acceptable). However, the pooled estimate for the CFI is quite low, only 0.91. Obviously, the pooling of indices in semTools/lavaan is not simply taking the average over alle imputed data sets.

In Enders Applied Missing Data Analysis (2010) it says that "there is no established method for pooling these indices" (page 251). So my question is, firstly, how is the pooling of fit indices done in semTools/lavaan? And secondly, are there possibilities to modify this method?

Best, Nathan

> > the standard errors were correct. When scale.W = TRUE, which is also the default, the pooling is done by some alternative method using ARIV, which apparently didn't work well in my case. However the standard pooling works just fine!
>
> Indeed, glad you figured this out already.  The single ARIV calculated using the entire parameter vector is theoretically more stable (see Enders, 2010), but I have noticed there are situations when it is problematic.  I think it is when standard RIVs (individual per parameter) vary wildly across parameters, but it might be something else, like near linear dependency of the within-imputation sampling covariance matrix.  Setting scale.W = FALSE sounds like the best thing to do.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
Ok. I thought you might have raw counts. Those never behave well . . .

So DWLS might be fine treating the outcome as continuous, depending on how much zero-inflation you have. If you also have a ceiling effect (some respondents marking "very often" to every item, you might run into more problems.

I suggest a sensitivity analysis, comparing the DWLS results with the continuous outcome against a binned outcome treated as ordinal. For example, the zeroes as one category, and the remaining values split into tertiles or quartiles (depending on how big the cells are, and/or a ceiling category if it's large enough). The comparison will help you determine whether the distribution is causing a problem.

Good luck!

Ah, I looked more closely.

The quadratic model should also include the linear slope. If you do that, your model will be under-identified because of too few occasions.

>
> So DWLS might be fine treating the outcome as continuous, depending on how much zero-inflation you have. If you also have a ceiling effect (some respondents marking "very often" to every item, you might run into more problems.

For example, the zeroes as one category, and the remaining values split into tertiles or quartiles (depending on how big the cells are, and/or a ceiling category if it's large enough). messages.subject: Re: Exploding Standard Errors with RunMI() respectively sem.mi()
messages.subject_clean: Exploding Standard Errors with RunMI() respectively sem.mi()
messages.body_plain:
I suspect that your imputations are just bad, or maybe you have so much missing data that your between-imputation variability dominates the within imputation variability. (It rarely if ever makes sense to look at the individual imputation results, IMHO. It does make sense though to look at the imputed data and check if the imputations make sense, see e.g. Bondarenko and Raghunathan 2016 https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.6926).

Also adapting scalar statistics, like R^2 in regression or fit indices SEM, for multiple imputations is not trivial. MI is primarily intended for point and variance estimation, and justifications for the fit-type statistics are done in hindsight, at best.

-- Stas Kolenikov, PhD, PStat (ASA, SSC)  @StatStas
-- Principal Scientist, Abt Associates @AbtDataScience
-- Opinions stated in this email are mine only, and do not reflect the position of my employer
-- http://stas.kolenikov.name

On Tue, May 25, 2021 at 4:07 AM Nathan Brack <brack.n...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear Terrence
>
> Thank you very much for your answer! I have another brief question concerning the pooling, but this time the pooling of goodness-of-fit indices.
>
> By accident, I found that for example the CFI for each single imputed set is around 0.95 to 0.96 (acceptable). However, the pooled estimate for the CFI is quite low, only 0.91. Obviously, the pooling of indices in semTools/lavaan is not simply taking the average over alle imputed data sets.
>
> In Enders Applied Missing Data Analysis (2010) it says that "there is no established method for pooling these indices" (page 251). So my question is, firstly, how is the pooling of fit indices done in semTools/lavaan? And secondly, are there possibilities to modify this method?
>
> Best, Nathan
>
> Terrence Jorgensen schrieb am Donnerstag, 29. April 2021 um 05:27:12 UTC+2:
> > > By putting the following argument
> > >
> > > summary(..., scale.W = FALSE)
> > >
> > > the standard errors were correct. When scale.W = TRUE, which is also the default, the pooling is done by some alternative method using ARIV, which apparently didn't work well in my case. However the standard pooling works just fine!
> >
> > Indeed, glad you figured this out already.  The single ARIV calculated using the entire parameter vector is theoretically more stable (see Enders, 2010), but I have noticed there are situations when it is problematic.  I think it is when standard RIVs (individual per parameter) vary wildly across parameters, but it might be something else, like near linear dependency of the within-imputation sampling covariance matrix.  Setting scale.W = FALSE sounds like the best thing to do.
> >
> > Terrence D. Jorgensen
> > Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> > Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
Mauricio,

Thanks again for your suggestions.

The multivariate simulation is a good idea. Unfortunately, it did not solve the problem. The latent mean and variance of T2 is still underestimated.

The cfa function fixes the item intercepts to zero. I thought that it was not a good idea to fix the intercepts while the thresholds and loadings are constrained equal over time. Shouldn't the item intercepts move along with the latent factor mean?

Berend

messages.body_plain:
Berend

Ok, I found how to make it work.
For invariance constraints for categorical items, you want to fix the intercepts of all the items to 0. This way it can estimate the latent mean at time 2.
Also, you want to fix the indicator variances at 1 at time 1 and estiate them at time 2.
Notice that these intercepts and variances are not for the indicators, but for the Latent Response Distribution for the underlying continuous distribtibution that gives rise to the categorical responses.
Finally, you want to use theta parameterization. With these changes I get the variance of 2 and mean of 0.5 at time 2, and correlation of 0.7

model <- '
   # Factors
   F1 =~ a1*Item_1+a2*Item_2+a3*Item_3+a4*Item_4+a5*Item_5+a6*Item_6+
         a7*Item_7+a8*Item_8+a9*Item_9+a10*Item_10
   F2 =~ a1*Item_1.1+a2*Item_2.1+a3*Item_3.1+a4*Item_4.1+a5*Item_5.1+
         a6*Item_6.1+a7*Item_7.1+a8*Item_8.1+a9*Item_9.1+a10*Item_10.1

   # Thresholds
   Item_1 + Item_1.1 | b11*t1+b12*t2+b13*t3
   Item_2 + Item_2.1 | b21*t1+b22*t2+b23*t3
   Item_3 + Item_3.1 | b31*t1+b32*t2+b33*t3
   Item_4 + Item_4.1 | b41*t1+b42*t2+b43*t3
   Item_5 + Item_5.1 | b51*t1+b52*t2+b53*t3
   Item_6 + Item_6.1 | b61*t1+b62*t2+b63*t3
   Item_7 + Item_7.1 | b71*t1+b72*t2+b73*t3
   Item_8 + Item_8.1 | b81*t1+b82*t2+b83*t3
   Item_9 + Item_9.1 | b91*t1+b92*t2+b93*t3
   Item_10 + Item_10.1 | b101*t1+b102*t2+b103*t3

   F1 ~~ 1*F1
   F2 ~~ NA*F2
   F1 ~~ NA*F2

   F1 ~ 0*1
   F2 ~NA*1

   Item_1.1 ~~ NA*Item_1.1
   Item_2.1 ~~ NA*Item_2.1
   Item_3.1 ~~ NA*Item_3.1
   Item_4.1 ~~ NA*Item_4.1
   Item_5.1 ~~ NA*Item_5.1
   Item_6.1 ~~ NA*Item_6.1
   Item_7.1 ~~ NA*Item_7.1
   Item_8.1 ~~ NA*Item_8.1
   Item_9.1 ~~ NA*Item_9.1
   Item_10.1 ~~ NA*Item_10.1
   '

fit <- cfa(model, data=datw, std.lv <http://std.lv>=T, ordered=T,
           parameterization="theta")
summary(fit, standardized=T)

messages.subject: Re: Cross levels regression in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Cross levels regression in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
> I want to test the effect of a level 2 latent variable on a level 1 latent variable with lavaan.

A level-2 outcome can only be explained by the level-2 component of a level-1 variable.

https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/a0020141

> Do you know if the current version of lavaan allows for this type of multilevel regressions?
>
> Something like
>
> model <- '
> level: 1
> fw =~ x1 + x2 + x3
>
> fw ~ fb
>
> level: 2
> fb ~ x1 + x2 + x3
> '

No, that makes no sense.  Any fw factor scores within the same cluster have the same value of fb, and fb cannot explain between-cluster differences in fw because there are none (within-level components are cluster-mean-centered by definition).  In Mplus, Level-1 parameters can vary across clusters, making the parameters Level-2 variables.  So, for example, fb could predict the variance of fw (if it is modeled as a random parameter across clusters).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Second-order latent factor growth curve models: Fixing the factor loadings vs. fixing the variances of the latent variables
messages.subject_clean: Second-order latent factor growth curve models: Fixing the factor loadings vs. fixing the variances of the latent variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I fitted a second-order latent factor growth curve model. The first order is a bi-factor model with four general factors (on_maintenance_numerical, on_maintenance_spatial, off_maintenance_numerical, and off_maintenance_spatial,) and two specific factors (on_intcontrol and off_intcontrol). The second order is a growth curve model in which the intercept and the slope act on the two specific factors. Strong measurement invariance is modeled. Here is the model:

## Cutting-edge alternative - multivariate growth curve modeling

m <- '# multivariate growth curve modeling

# 1. First order latent variables - bi-factor model  (weak invariance)

on_maintenance_numerical =~  b10*on_csnumerical + b1*on_updatingnumerical + b2*on_ssnumerical + b3*on_ssverbal

on_maintenance_spatial =~ b11*on_csspatial +  b4*on_updatingspatial + b5*on_ssspatial + b6*on_ssarrow

on_intcontrol =~  b12*on_csnumerical + b7*on_csspatial + b8*on_updatingnumerical + b9*on_updatingspatial

off_maintenance_numerical =~  b10*off_csnumerical + b1*off_updatingnumerical + b2*off_ssnumerical + b3*off_ssverbal

off_maintenance_spatial =~ b11*off_csspatial +  b4*off_updatingspatial + b5*off_ssspatial + b6*off_ssarrow

off_intcontrol =~  b12*off_csnumerical + b7*off_csspatial + b8*off_updatingnumerical + b9*off_updatingspatial

#2. Fixing the reference indicators’ intercepts at zero

on_csnumerical ~ 0*1

on_csspatial ~ 0*1

off_csnumerical ~ 0*1

off_csspatial ~ 0*1

#3. Do not estimate (i.e. fix at zero) the first-order latent variable means

on_maintenance_numerical ~ 0*1

on_maintenance_spatial ~ 0*1

on_intcontrol ~ 0*1

off_maintenance_numerical ~ 0*1

off_maintenance_spatial ~ 0*1

off_intcontrol ~ 0*1

#4. Constrain the other indicators’ intercepts to strong time equivalence (invariance)

on_updatingnumerical ~ w1*1

on_ssnumerical ~ w2*1

on_ssverbal ~ w3*1

on_updatingspatial ~ w4*1

on_ssspatial ~ w5*1

on_ssarrow ~ w6*1

off_updatingnumerical ~ w1*1

off_ssnumerical ~ w2*1

off_ssverbal ~ w3*1

off_updatingspatial ~ w4*1

off_ssspatial ~ w5*1

off_ssarrow ~ w6*1

#5.1 Measurement error autocorrelations

on_ssnumerical ~~ off_ssnumerical

on_ssverbal ~~ off_ssverbal

on_ssspatial ~~ off_ssspatial

on_ssarrow ~~ off_ssarrow

on_csnumerical ~~ off_csnumerical

on_updatingnumerical ~~ off_updatingnumerical

on_csspatial ~~ off_csspatial

on_updatingspatial ~~ off_updatingspatial

#5.2 Fix to zero latent correlations because of bi-factor modeling

on_maintenance_numerical ~~ 0*on_intcontrol

on_maintenance_spatial ~~ 0*on_intcontrol

off_maintenance_numerical ~~ 0*off_intcontrol

off_maintenance_spatial ~~ 0*off_intcontrol

on_maintenance_numerical ~~ 0*off_intcontrol

on_maintenance_spatial ~~ 0*off_intcontrol

off_maintenance_numerical ~~ 0*on_intcontrol

off_maintenance_spatial ~~ 0*on_intcontrol

#6. Second-order factors of the linear model

i_intcontrol =~ 1*off_intcontrol + 1*on_intcontrol

s_intcontrol =~ 0*off_intcontrol + 1*on_intcontrol

i_maintenance_numerical =~ 1*off_maintenance_numerical + 1*on_maintenance_numerical

s_maintenance_numerical =~ 0*off_maintenance_numerical + 1*on_maintenance_numerical

i_maintenance_spatial =~ 1*off_maintenance_spatial + 1*on_maintenance_spatial

s_maintenance_spatial =~ 0*off_maintenance_spatial + 1*on_maintenance_spatial

# 6.2 Fix to zero the correlations between the first-order factors, the slope and intercept factors

on_intcontrol ~~ 0*i_maintenance_numerical

on_intcontrol ~~ 0*s_maintenance_numerical

on_intcontrol ~~ 0*i_maintenance_spatial

on_intcontrol ~~ 0*s_maintenance_spatial

on_maintenance_numerical ~~ 0*i_intcontrol

on_maintenance_numerical ~~ 0*s_intcontrol

on_maintenance_numerical ~~ 0*i_maintenance_spatial

on_maintenance_numerical ~~ 0*s_maintenance_spatial

on_maintenance_spatial ~~ 0*i_intcontrol

on_maintenance_spatial ~~ 0*s_intcontrol

on_maintenance_spatial ~~ 0*i_maintenance_numerical

on_maintenance_spatial ~~ 0*s_maintenance_numerical

off_intcontrol ~~ 0*i_maintenance_numerical

off_intcontrol ~~ 0*s_maintenance_numerical

messages.body_plain:
###

First, am I right to believe that the means and intercepts of latent variables are arbitrary (in my case with the variance of the intercept and slope fixed to 1) and not directly interpretable (e.g. the intercept is not the mean of time point one)?

####
the factor means are arbitrary based on the identification method you used. With fixed variance/mean method the means witll be 0 at time 1 and (after strong invariance) for the next times points will be in reference to the mean change compared to time 1. The intercept of growth curve is the average score at which time point you set the 0 in the time scale. This is also arbitrary as you can choose where to set your time 0. But this growth curve is interpretable, most commonly as the mean at the first time point, or start point of the longitudinal change

###

Second, I have been asked to compare my linear growth model to intercept-only and curvilinear models to provide a rationale for this approach.

###
The intercept only model will be done by excluding any other factor slopes, just one growth factor.
The linear model, would have the intercept factor, and the linear slope factors
The quadratic model would have, the intercept, linear and quadratic factors
Would recommend this book for these other extensions of models
Grimm, K. J., Ram, N., & Estabrook, R. (2016). Growth Modeling: Structural Equation and Multilevel Modeling Approaches.
A quadratic factor is consider a higher order term. This means that for estimating any higher order terms, you need to include all previous lower order terms, in this case, linear and intercept factors

Op woensdag 26 mei 2021 om 02:20:24 UTC+2 schreef mauga...@gmail.com:

> Berend
>
> Ok, I found how to make it work.
> For invariance constraints for categorical items, you want to fix the intercepts of all the items to 0. This way it can estimate the latent mean at time 2.
> Also, you want to fix the indicator variances at 1 at time 1 and estiate them at time 2.
> Notice that these intercepts and variances are not for the indicators, but for the Latent Response Distribution for the underlying continuous distribtibution that gives rise to the categorical responses.
> Finally, you want to use theta parameterization. With these changes I get the variance of 2 and mean of 0.5 at time 2, and correlation of 0.7
>
>
> model <- '
>    # Factors
>    F1 =~ a1*Item_1+a2*Item_2+a3*Item_3+a4*Item_4+a5*Item_5+a6*Item_6+
>          a7*Item_7+a8*Item_8+a9*Item_9+a10*Item_10
>    F2 =~ a1*Item_1.1+a2*Item_2.1+a3*Item_3.1+a4*Item_4.1+a5*Item_5.1+
>          a6*Item_6.1+a7*Item_7.1+a8*Item_8.1+a9*Item_9.1+a10*Item_10.1
>
>    # Thresholds

Hi everyone,

I am a bit confused regarding the estimator choice when developing a SEM mode.

Specifically, I can't decide between the WLSMV and MLR/MLM options. My data are non-normal and the dependent variable is a latent variable with continuous indicators. messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm testing for longitudinal measurement invariance across three time points but the models at each stage of the invariance test (i.e. baseline, loading invariance, and threshold invariance) are all being flagged with the warning: "covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite". When I inspect the covariance matrix and the corresponding correlation matrix, I find that the correlations for factor 1 across the three time points are all greater than 1 (e.g., correlating factor 1 at time 1 with factor 1 at time 2).

So that appears to be the problem causing the warning. My question is what I should do about that? Do I need to change the model specification in some way or can I ignore the warning and interpret the change in model fit across the three models?

The cfa model I'm testing is a 2-factor solution from a measure with 14 items (four items load on factor 1 and the other ten load on factor 2) over three time periods with a sample size of 722 (the sample size is lower at the second and third time points). My syntax is adapted from the supplemental materials from this article: https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000075 <https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/met0000075>

Any help would be much appreciated.

Regards
Simon

approach 2: fixing to 1 the variances of all the latent variables.
In this case, I used the following code: fit <- lavaan::growth(m, data = tmp, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)
and I got a model with acceptable fit statistics

For me, it is unclear why the results are different. I suppose that this has something to do with the second-order growth curve aspect of the model. When only fitting the bi-factor model (first order), the results are simialr across both approches.

messages.subject: lavaan factor scores to feed other models
messages.subject_clean: lavaan factor scores to feed other models
messages.body_plain:
Let's suppose I have an outcome variable that is not continuous. For example, it could be an ordered categorical variable or a nominal (unordered) categorical variable. This implies that I would need to model the variable as an ordered logit model or as a multinomial model.

I know lavaan and other softwares does not include the option to fit a whole structural equation model SEM with outcome variables that are not continuous (there is only a workaround for binary variables). As I would like to still use latent variables in the categorical model, I was wondering if it is correct to calculate the factor scores using the lavPredict() function and just include these latent variables as regressors in an external categorical model. I have seen many examples where people follow this approach but using Exploratory Factor Analysis EFA or Principal Component Analysis PCA. I would preper to rely on CFA since I do have a clear and solid theory about the latent variables.

Moreover, the lavPredict() function has the argument method with the options regression and Bartlett. Should I use the regression or the Bartlett factor scores? what are the differences among the two alternatives?

In other words:
    library(lavaan) HS.model <- '
                   visual =~ x1 + x2 + x3
                  textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
                  speed =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
    fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)
     Latents <- lavPredict(fit)
     Latents <- as.data.frame(Latents)
     Latents_Bartlett <- lavPredict(fit, method = "Bartlett")
      Latents_Bartlett <- as.data.frame(Latents_Bartlett)

It is correct to use the latent variables visual, textual, and speed in the dataframes Latents or Latents_Bartlett as regressors in a subsequent ordered logit model or multinomial model?

messages.body_plain:
This seems like an issue of the R sessions not knowing the summary types.

Can be caused if you are not loading semTools with library(semTools). So if you call the function like semTools::compareFit(), R will called the right function even if semTools hasent being loaded, but R doesnt have the summary method because you havent loaded the package

My recommendation, have the run it with the library line, and without the semTools:: , this way you will be sure that they are using the loaded functions. Because of they havent loaded the package it will tell them that there is no compareFit function
